claims.text: Spin-polarized DFT can be used to assess the presence of a ferromagnetic ground state in itinerant-electron or transition-metal systems.
A ferromagnetic ground state is predicted when the spin-aligned solution has lower total energy than the non-spin-polarized solution.
A paramagnetic or non-spin-polarized electronic configuration is typical of the initial state used for a transition-metal or itinerant-electron system.
LDA and GGA functionals can be used as exchange-correlation functionals in electronic-structure total-energy calculations.
The cited calculation should be made spin-polarized.
LSDA or GGA can be tailored or selected specifically for magnetic systems.
The relevant comparison is a zero-temperature ground-state calculation between spin-polarized and non-spin-polarized solutions.
Explicit treatment of exchange and correlation produces exchange splitting of the electronic states or density of states.
Spin-polarized DFT explicitly accounts for electron-exchange interactions.
Electron-exchange interactions stabilize the spin-aligned ferromagnetic configuration relative to the non-magnetic configuration.
The spin-polarized calculation will have lower total energy than the non-spin-polarized calculation.
The spin-polarized calculation will yield a finite magnetic moment.
Lower total energy together with a finite magnetic moment indicates stabilization of a ferromagnetic state relative to the spin-unpolarized solution.
A non-spin-polarized DFT calculation does not represent exchange splitting and therefore gives a higher total energy for the same system.
The proposed behavior is expected only when exchange interactions are sufficiently strong and the chosen functional adequately captures electronic correlation.
Standard functionals may be inadequate for systems with strong electronic correlations.
The predicted energy difference and magnetic moment depend on the material and exchange-correlation functional.
If the non-spin-polarized state has equal or lower energy and the spin-polarized state has no significant finite magnetic moment, the proposed stabilization criterion is falsified.
